industries_compared: healthcare-assistant; hr-recruitment; education-ai-tutor; content-creator; mobility-autonomous-driving; media-news-social-political-assistant
recurring_harms: injury (direct physical harm from incorrect medical recommendations); discrimination (algorithmic bias perpetuating healthcare disparities); opportunity loss (delayed diagnosis and treatment)
common_failure_layers: data (training data reflecting historical biases and inequities); governance-process (missing oversight protocols, inadequate validation, insufficient regulatory compliance)
human_in_loop_decisions: Every medical diagnosis or treatment recommendation requires physician verification. Every rejection in hiring requires appeal mechanism. Every autonomous vehicle decision requires human override capability. Every content moderation decision requires human review for context. Every financial decision requires compliance checkpoint.
strongest_guardrails: Physician or expert review requirement with documented authority and liability framework. Mandatory escalation for high-stakes outcomes with defined response times. Demographic parity testing and fairness auditing across all protected groups. Human-in-the-loop with documented override authority and decision trails.
cross_industry_pattern: AI systems trained on historical data perpetuate existing biases regardless of industry. This is demonstrated in healthcare (racial bias in clinical algorithms), HR (gender bias in resume screening), and education (socioeconomic bias in student assessment). The common pattern is that training data reflects systemic inequities that AI systems learn and amplify. Governance process failures rather than model failures are the primary root cause in most documented incidents: the Watson case shows a $4 billion system fail not from technical limitation but from inadequate validation and unrealistic expectations. The Theranos case shows catastrophic harm from governance failures (no quality management, no independent validation) rather than AI limitations per se. Human oversight without authority, time, and information is insufficient - rubber-stamp reviews do not constitute meaningful control. The strongest guardrails across all industries are those with clear accountability, defined thresholds, automatic escalation, and continuous monitoring rather than periodic review.
